496: The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence in each case to one for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that (i) the convictions should be maintained; (ii) the sentence should not have been imposed on the appellants because they had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge; and (iii) the evidence of the eye witnesses was unreliable. Held, that the convictions must be set aside. The evidence of the eyewitnesses was reliable and there was no reason why the evidence of a single witness should not be accepted. The evidence given by the eye witnesses could not be rejected merely because they did not give the names of the assailants. The evidence was admissible only if the number of persons who gave the injuries was more than the number of assailants. The statement made by the eye witness was not an independent piece of evidence. The evidence relating to the incident was admissible only when it was shown that the assailants were armed with weapons.

The Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore state from the profits accruing or arising in that State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court erred in holding that the bank was not entitled to set off the loss incurred by the assessee in Travancore State because the bank had no branch within the State of Cochin and the assessee had no branch outside the State. [817 E] Commissioner of Income tax vs Kedarnath Chunder & Sons, ; , followed.
232: The respondent was charged with various offences and convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment. He filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed his appeal on the ground that there was no reasonable classification between him and others, and that the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of warrant cases by a special court was discriminatory in so far as it authorised the State Government to direct that certain offences or classes of offences or classes should be tried by a special judge. Held, that the provisions of section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution because the procedure prescribed under the Code of 1898 had not been followed in the case of the respondent. The procedure laid down in the Code of 1973 was applicable only where the accused person was being tried at the commencement of the trial and not where the trial was commenced after the commencement of this Act. The procedure prescribed by section 5(1) of Act XXXI of 1949 did not apply to the trial of warrant case by a special magistrate.

3019: The petitioner Rao gave a somewhat different version of what had happened. He did not assist Kumari Prakash to go away from his parents ' house. At the hearing of the petition Rao gave a very different version of how he came into possession of the property in dispute and that he was in possession thereof. The Central Gove rnment, however, rejected the plea. The High Court held that the petitioner was guilty of misconduct under section 19 of the Army Act and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The rule given by the Central Government is an independent power. If the Central Government has exercised its powers under section 19 it cannot be said that the Central Government acted without authority or jurisdiction. [839 E] (2) The Central Government can remove an officer from service under section 19 if it finds that the officer concerned is guilty of any of the acts specified in section 19. Section 19 does not use the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" but only uses the words "without prejudice to the generality of the power conferred by sub section 2(a)." [839 F] (3) The Central Goverrnment could have removed the petitioner from service under s. 19 if it found that the officer was guilty of any act specified in section 18. But the Central Government did not do so. [840 B C] (4) The Central Govt. could not take action under section 19 on the ground that the officer had committed some other act which was not mentioned in section 18 of the Army Rules, 1954. [841 D]

7130: The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and injunction filed by the respondents. [1021C] 3.1 The question whether the suit was maintainable or not depends upon the nature of the relief claimed. [1022D] 3.2 The High Court was right in holding that the decree was not sustainable. 6270: The respondent was appointed as Secretary, Zila Sainik Board, Unnao on 20th August, 1979. He was not satisfied by the order of appointment issued in his favour and he preferred a Review Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service on the pronouncement of the Judgment on 24th March, 1988 which in the circumstances could not have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the High Court to dispose of the Writ Petition on merits. The High Courts were right in holding that the High Court was right in making an order on Review on 26.7.1988 relying upon the interim order dated 10.7.1986 which in the circumstance could not have been made by the Governor. [244E F]

1531: The respondents were partners in a firm carrying on business as commission agents and also as partners in a partnership firm. In the assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55, the Income tax Officer assessed the amounts received by the heirs and legal representatives of the deceased persons as income under section 34(1) (b) read with section 24B of the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessments for the years 1950 51 and 1951 52 were quashed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the assessments could not be made on the realisations. On appeal to this Court, HELD : The provisions of section 24B are mandatory and not directory. The words "if any person dies before the publication of the public notice" in sub section (2) of section 22 or section 34 must mean "the heir or legal representative of a deceased person". The words "or if he dies after making the return" in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 24A must mean "any person who has died before the publication." The word 'heirs ' is used in the same sense in sub sections (3) and (4). The words "any person" in sub clauses (a), (b) and (c) of section 24 B must mean "all the heirs and Legal Representatives of a deceased Hindu dying after the publication of a public notice under section 22 or 34". The words 'any person' in sub sections I, 2 and 4 must mean "an heir or legal representatives of a deceased male Hindu dying after his death ". The words "who has died before publication of the notice" in subsec tion (2) must mean "a heir or legal representatio nal representative of a dead person". [708 F] In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, , referred to.

1974: The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. He had two sons, namely, Sri Ram and Sri Ram. The assessee was the sole surviving son of Sri Ram. In the year 1949, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ from the Government as an allowance during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the alleged cash grant of varying and unspecified amount received by the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act and that the said amount was not liable to be taxed under the Indian Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal held that the sum of Rs 36,391/ was chargeable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act as income derived from the land revenue of the Seyedpur village. The High Court on reference confirmed the decision of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "agricultural income" has been used in the sense of income derived from property held for the purpose of agriculture or as income derived by a person from any source whatsoever. [172B] 2. The expression 'income derived from property so long as it subsists does not include agricultural income. [174C] 3. The expression has been used with reference to agricultural income only. It includes agricultural income also. [175D] 4. The expression means agricultural income. The expression is used in the context of income derived by way of interest on securities. The expression must be understood in its popular sense as having reference to the income derived from land. [177E] 5. The expression in the context must mean income derived from lands. [178F] 6. The expression does not refer to agricultural income but refers to income derived from other sources. The expression may have reference to income derived by rendering services or rendering services. But the expression does not necessarily refer to income derived or rendered. [179G]
1778: The appellant company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It is a subsidiary of the appellant company. The appellant company entered into an agreement with its workmen for the supply of certain machinery and equipment to the respondent company. The agreement provided that the company would pay to the workmen at the rate of Rs. 1.25 per day as wages for every day of the month during which the machinery or equipment was not in use. The appellant paid to the workmen the amount specified in the agreement. The workmen were paid wages at the rate specified in the award. The appellant contended that the wages prescribed by the award did amount to wages as defined by section 2(vi) of the Act before it was amended. Held, that the wages fixed by the award could not be included in the definition of wages under section 2(v) of the , and the wage structure prescribed by the said award could not fall within the definition of "workman" under section 2 (vi). The unamended definition of wages given by section 2 (iv) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was applicable to the case, because the terms of the contract between the parties when they deal with disputes arising between them in respect of the said terms, were governed by the terms of contract between the employer and the employees. The unamendment clause in section 2(iv) of Act, 1947 was not intended to apply to the case where the terms of employment were governed by a statute.

[176 F G] (4) The expression 'officer or employee ' in sub sec. (1) must be construed in its popular sense as meaning a person who has been appointed to any office or post either under the Government or under the Central or State Government. He made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok Kumar for the month of May 1969, even though Asho k Kumar was not working in that Division. 6118: The petitioners are carpenters employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corporation") and are given all benefits due to them under the various labour legislations. They seek a direction from this Court for the regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act, 1948 and as such, the petitioners are entitled to be treated as industrial workmen and they have been paid the same wages as are payable to regular employees. The petitioners ' claim is that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work. The respondent Corporation contested the petition on the ground that the unit in which the petition qumstances were registered was not a factory registered within the meaning of the Factories Act. [712C] 3. The petitioners have no right to ask for regularisation of their service. [713D] 4. The petitioners do not have any vested right to get the benefit of the minimum wage fixed by the Deputy Com missioner. [714E] 5. The petitioners' claim is misconceived. [715F]

Court was wrong in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the trial court. [806 D]
4938: The appellant was a money lender. He carried on business as a money lenders and had obtained a licence under the U.P. Excise Act, 1910. The licence was renewed for a period of one year from 1st April, 1961 to 31st March, 1962. The appellant 's licence expired on 30th September, 1963. The Administrator issued a notice dated 27th October, 1964 calling upon the appellant to show cause why he should not be prosecuted for having committed an offence punishable under section 27(1)(a) of the U. P. Excise Act. The appellant filed his reply on 28th November, 1964. The Administrator passed an order on 29th December, 1965 directing that the appellant should be prosecuted for an offence punishable with imprisonment for two years or more. The appellant challenged the validity of this order in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was contended that (i) the Administrator has no power to grant permission to carry on money lending business; (ii) the Administrator is not empowered to exercise the power conferred on him under sec. 27(6) of the Act; (iii) the Administrator cannot delegate his functions to another person; (iv) the Administrator can exercise the power delegated to him only when he is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for doing so. [881 G] (iii) The Administrator can exercise his powers under sec.27(6) only when he considers that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of an offence. 3844: The plaintiff filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses, a land, two shops, leaving a portion of the joint family properties. The trial court held that the properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. On appeal by the defendants, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court on the ground that the properties were joint family property and that the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the joint family property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court erred in holding that the properties did not belong to the joint Hindu family, that there was no prior partition between himself and his two sons, that the plaintiff 's claim was barred by limitation, and that the suit was barred by res judicata. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was nothing in the deed of partition which prevented the plaintiff from claiming partition. [766 C] (2) The plaintiff 's share in the properties was not partitioned during his lifetime but was given to his wife and children. The plaintiff ' s wife had no right to claim partition. She had only a life interest in the properties. The plaintiff could not claim partition as a matter of right. [767 D E] (3) The plaintiff was entitled under section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act to a share of the joint property. The plaintiff was therefore entitled to a 1/4th share in the property. [768 F] (4) The plaintiff is entitled to a 7/23rd share in the suit properties. The High Court rightly refused to add 1/4 th share to the plaintiff ' s share. [769 A B] (5) The plaintiff has been able to prove that the properties in question belonged to him. He has also proved that he had partitioned them during his lifetime. The plaintiff has failed to prove that he had separated from his father during his lifetime, nor has he produced any evidence to show that he had separately acquired the properties. [770 H]

In the year 1956, the appellant company entered into a contract with the respondent company for the sale of certain goods manufactured by it. The contract provided that the goods would be sold at the factory gate at Delhi. The respondent company paid the price of the goods to the appellant company at Delhi. On the same day, the appellant Company sold the goods to its customers in Delhi. The appellant company also sold the goods in Delhi. 5141: The Karnataka State Transport Authority granted permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, one permit to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to the Bangalore Tourism Development Corporation. A number of appeals were preferred to the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63(7), the applications from the 'non preferred category had to be excluded as the number of applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number of permits to be granted. It was on this ground that the grant of two permits to Karnataka State Tourism Corporation was set aside, though the Appellate Tribunal had no doubt regarding the resources and ability of that Corporation to operate the tourist services. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the State Transport Authority could not have been made a party to the proceedings before the Tribunal. [146C] 2. The proviso to section 3(1) of the Act is an enabling provision which enables the State Government to make rules for regulating the grant of permits. The proviso does not confer any power upon the State Government under section 63(2). The proviso only confers a power on the State Government when it considers necessary to make rules or orders in respect of the matters covered by section 63(1). The proviso cannot be read as conferring a power on a State Government to frame rules or regulations with retrospective effect. [144B C] 3. The proviso is intended to enable the State Government in making rules or regulations framed under section 63 (2) to regulate the grant of stage carriage permits. The State Government can make rules or regulations in respect of such matters as may be prescribed. The proviso cannot therefore be construed as conferring a right on the State Transport Undertaking to issue permits to the private operators. [144D E] 4. The proviso requires that the State Government should consider the need for granting permits to the State Transport Undertakings. The proviso has to be read along with the proviso. The proviso must be read as a whole. [145E F] 5. The proviso applies only to cases where the State Transport undertaking is a State Transport Undertaking. The proviso will apply only to cases in which the State Transport undertakings are a State Transport undertaking. [145F G] 6
2593: The appellant was a Government servant in the State of Bombay. He was dismissed from service by an order dated February 2, 1955. The question for determination was whether he could be said to have been dismissed under article 311(2) of the Constitution on account of his being a Government servant within the meaning of article 311(1). Held, that the appellant was not entitled to claim arrears of salary and the State of Maharashtra had no right to recover it as such. The State of Bombay was not a Government servant but a Government servant. The State Government was not bound to pay him any arrears of salary or other dues which may become due to him before the appointed day. The State was not bound by the terms of the contract between the parties. The State had no right whatsoever to recover the arrears of salary payable to the appellant after the appointed day, nor did the State have any right to recover the same. The State could not claim the arrears of wages or other dues of the appellant after he ceased to be Government servant.
1789: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947 under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had a branch office at Calcutta and its branches were situated within the jurisdiction of the Bombay High Court. In July, 1947 it converted into a public limited company. On September 9, 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing medical examination on reaching the age of 55. The Tribunal has found that the age fixed at 60 would be applicable only to those employees who have been confirmed in the Bombay and Bombay regions. The Tribunal had therefore correctly come to the conclusion that the age at which the employees should retire should be fixed. [440 D E] (iii)In the Bombay region there are two different grades of employees. One is the pay scale of the employees at Bombay and the other is the pay scales of the employees of the Bombay region. The pay scales of employees at Bombay region are different from those of the employees in Bombay region. There is no difference in the pay scales between the two regions. The employees of Bombay region are entitled to equal pay. [441 F H; 442 A B] (iv)The Tribunal was right in holding that the age prescribed in Bombay region should be fixed in the Gujarat region. [443 G]
3531: The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of glass bottles. It had a factory at Baroda, and its workmen were employed as watchmen. The workmen were paid wages for one day only. The workmen claimed that they should be given sick leave on the ground that they were not qualified to claim sickness benefit under the provisions of the Act. The workmen contended that the Act provided more than adequate sickness benefits and any additional benefit would place unproductive financial burden on the industry and would have an all round adverse effect on other industries. The Tribunal held that the Act did not provide more than sufficient sickness benefits but it also found that the workmen were entitled to sickness benefit under section 2(1) (g) of the , and that the workmen could not be denied the benefit of sick leave. On appeal by the workmen, the Industrial Tribunal held that there was no justification for granting sick leave to the workmen. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal has erred in holding that the workmen are entitled to sick leave. [711C] 2. The Act provides more than sufficient sick leave. The Act does not provide for any further grant of sick leave or leave of absence. The Act is intended to give relief to the workmen who are unable to avail themselves of sick leave due to sickness. [712B] 3. The Act makes provision for sickness benefit to workmen who are prevented from availing themselves of sick Leave. The Act also makes provision for sick leave to workmen who have been granted sick leave. Section 2(1)(g) of which defines sick leave to mean "a person qualified to claim a sickness benefit". The Act also provides for sick leave. It also provides for sickness benefit. [713D E] 4. The Act gives benefit of sickness to workmen who do not get any benefit under the Act. [714E] 5. The Act clearly lays down that sickness benefit shall be available to the workmen if they are prevented from doing so due to sickness, accident or natural calamities. The Act further provides that sick leave shall be available only to those workmen who are able to obtain such leave. [752F] 6. The Act, therefore, cannot be said to be providing more than sufficient for the workmen to claim sickness.
5397: The petitioner was a temporary employee of the Ministry of Works and Housing. [767C D] 2.3 The appropriate authority can exercise power under cl.(j) in case of a government servant in Class I or Class II service or post where it has exercised power under clause(j) in respect of a Government Servant in Class II or Class II Service, after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service. [768E F]
5937: The petitioners, who were manufacturing grey cloth and fabric, claimed that they should be treated as 'manufacturers ' for the purpose of determining their assessable value. They contended that the processor 's expenses, costs and charges including the cost of the grey fabrics would be included in the price at which the gre y cloth was sold by the processor. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the processer 's expenses and costs were included in the assessable value of the processed fabric and excise duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at whose sale the goods must be selling the processed goods in the market would include only the price at what is the price atwhich the processor would leave the processor's factory plus his profit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The processor ' 's expenses are included in the value of the processing and excise duty. [326C] 2. The processors ' expenses, cost and charges are included in their profits and expenses. [327E] 3. The processer ' 's expense, costs and expenses are included when he goes into the processor "s expenses, cost or charges plus profit, but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. [331F] 4. The processter 's expenses have to be excluded from the assessable value. [332G] 5. The processo's expenses, costs & charges are included when the processor himself takes delivery of the goods from the processor and gets them back after taking delivery. [334A]
3602: The petitioner was appointed as a Forest Officer in the Mysore State. He retired from service on 31st December, 1966. After his retirement he filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for quashing the final list of officers prepared by the State Government. The Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner had not been heard before the final list was published and that the petitioner 's claim to have a copy of the final list prepared after hearing objections against the preliminary list was premature. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the Tribunal erred in law in holding that the final list should be prepared after hearing the objections; (ii) the Tribunal could not go behind the final list; (iii) the petitioner had no opportunity to object to the final list. HELD: (1) The Tribunal has rightly held that the petitioner was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him. [741C] (2) The Tribunal was right in holding that there was no violation of principles of natural justice. [742E] (3) The Tribunal had rightly held that there was non compliance with the principles of natural jus tice. [743A] (4) The Tribunal could not have gone into the question whether the final list had been published or not. The Tribunal had correctly decided that the petitioner could not be heard at all. [744B] (5) The Tribunal did not consider the merits of the case. It is true that the petitioner admitted that the Mysore State Civil Services Integration Rules provided for filing of objections against the final list but the Tribunal did not say anything about the merits of his case. [745D]
362: The respondent, a citizen of India, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 51. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 calling upon him to show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the demand. The assessee did not appear before the Income Tax Officer but his case was that the amount of arrears due from him had been paid up by him and that the recovery certificate issued by the Additional Collector was without authority of law. The Income tax Officer issued a certificate under section 46(2) of the Income tax Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the certificate was invalid as it was issued after the expiry of the period prescribed by article 226 of the Constitution. He also held that the recovery proceedings were barred by article 22(1) of the Constitution and that the certificate could not be issued under article 134A of the Constitution because the certificate was issued after expiry of the time limit prescribed by article 21. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of article 226 are designed to confer powers on the High Courts to issue writs and directions and they are meant to serve public interest and to serve the ends of justice. [766 C] (ii)The power conferred on the High Court is wide enough to enable it to issue writs or directions which may give relief to the citizens or even to an individual. It cannot be said that the High Court has no jurisdiction to issue a writ of certiorari when the revenue authorities have failed to exercise their jurisdiction properly. [767 D E] (iii)The High Court can issue a writ only if there is a statutory provision in the statute conferring the power to issue such a writ. If there is a specific provision in the Statute itself conferring the power, the remedy provided therein is not to enforce them. But if there is some other provision in the Act which confers the power on the High court to issue a Writ, then the High Court cannot issue a writ directing the authorities to do something which is contrary to law. [768 B C] (iv)The High Courts have been invested with inherent powers under article 226 of Constitution to issue writs as are necessary for enforcement
4963: The Wealth Tax Officer, in computing the wealth of a Hindu undivided family under the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, adopted the value of the interest on the capital asset of the assessee. In appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, the Tribunal held that the interest was liable to be included in the wealth of the assessee and dismissed the appeals. He could only adopt the method which would have been known to him if he were alive. [32B C] (3) The method of valuation is not unknown to law. It is open to the Wealth Tax Officer to adopt any other method or method. But where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price which in the opinion of the Wealth Tax officer would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. When the asset is a cash, its valuation date is the last day of the previous year as defined in clause (i). [34D E] (5) The Wealth 'Tax Officer cannot add to the valuation date a sum of money which is not payable by the assessee. If the assessee is entitled to receive back the amount paid by him, then the value of such amount will be reduced by the amount actually paid by him. [35F G] (6) The Wealthtax Officer can ignore the provisions of the Wealth 'Tax Act and the Wealth Tax Rules while determining the net wealth of the deceased. [36A B] (7) The Wealth, tax Officer is not competent to add to or reduce the valuation of the assessee's interest in the assets of an assessee. [37C] (8) The Wealth Act does not contemplate any addition to the value. [

6276: The petitioners in these petitions were lessees of a quarry lease for black granite and for quarrying stones. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1966 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, hereinafter referred to as the Rules, with effect from 1 7 1985 substituting the original rule 21 of the Rules by a new rule which reads as follows: "21. Royalty in respect of minor minerals known as Black Trap and Hard Murrum at Rs.7 per metric tonne by amending schedule of the rules which was being levied at Rs.4 till the date of the said amendment." 2727: The appellant was a hereditary trustee of the temple. He died in the year 1928 and his successor was appointed as a trustee. In 1950, the appellant filed a suit for setting aside the order of the Deputy Commissioner holding that the trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was a shebait within the meaning of section 6(9) of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property; it is an office of profit under the Hindu Law. It is a Shebait and he can be removed by the founder or his successor. [801 B] (2) The office is hereditary and the right to succeed to the office is regulated by usage or custom. The office is not hereditary. [802 C D] (3) The office must be transmitted to the founder either by appointment or by nomination. [803 E] (4) The office may be hereditary only if it is attached to the office. If it is attached there is no necessity to appoint a person to the office who has been appointed. [804 A] (5) The office cannot be regarded as hereditary merely because it is attached thereto. [805 G] (6) The office does not cease to be hereditary merely because the founder has appointed somebody else to perform the duties attached to the post. [806 B]

The evidence of PW 4 who was afflicted with the fell disease of leprosy cannot be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness might not have seen him in the company of the accused. The High 'Court was right in holding that the evidence was not reliable because of the fact that the witness had stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant. 2609: The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. 1522: The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post office. He had stole six registered letters and he fabricated three receipts showing that the registered letters were received by the addressees. The appellant 's father, who was a post man attached to the post office, was not in possession of any of these articles. The appellant was convicted under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 for offences under sections 465 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year in each case. The High Court set aside his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letter was recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives the greatest possible inference could be drawn against him that he was in possession of the article. The evidence shows that the appellant was in possession and that he was not in the house at all. [412 E F]

1378: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which set aside his conviction and sentence on the ground that the extra judicial confession made by him to a Police Officer was inadmissible in evidence as it was not proved that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. Held, that the extrajudicial confession of the appellant was admissible in evidence against the appellant. The evidence of the witnesses who gave the prosecution case about the recovery of the swords from the house of the appellant could not be rejected on the ground of non examination of independent witnesses. The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to the recovery of sword at the instance of the appellant. 3168: The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1950 under the Companies Act, 1913. It had a total number of 26,000 shares and its share capital was Rs. 1,00,000. In the year 1953, the company received a sum of Rs. 2,00,050 as balance sheet from the Registrar of Companies on account of the balance sheet for the year 1953 and on account of profit and loss account for the year 1954. 4568: The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Central Health Service on September 5, 1966. On April 2, 1971 he was called by the Banaras Hindu University for an interview for the post of Associate Professor. The appellant was not eligible for appointment or promotion as a Professor. The Central Health Service Rules, 1963 were framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution and the appellant was appointed to the post. The appellant challenged the validity of the rules before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant was not qualified for appointment or promoted as a Professor and that the rules were not framed till the year 1963. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the rules had been framed after the appellant had been selected by the Selection Committee constituted under the Rules and that the appellant could not be denied the benefit of the rules because they were made only for the purpose of filling up vacancies which arose in the year 1973. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant was entitled to be considered for promotion to the post in question. [263C] (2) The appellant is not only holding the post of Radiologist in the Indian Medical Service but also actively associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an Associate Professor of the Delhi University. 2440: The appellant company was a small scale industry in the State of Orissa. In respect of some of its concerns, it had fixed minimum wages for the workmen and also for the employees. The Tribunal held that there was no similar industry in the region in which minimum wage is higher than the minimum wage for the workmen. If the Tribunal finds that the industry is not providing any amenities which are different from the facilities available to the industry in the particular region, it will be doing something more than fixing the minimum wage. The Tribunal could not have done so because the Company was not paying minimum wage at all. It would be appropriate to take into account the fact that in the region, there are several industries in the same region, and the Tribunal has to consider the minimum wage in the case of such industries as well. 2913: The respondent assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 on a total income of Rs. 69,886/ and the Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961. 1697: The appellant was a partner in a firm carrying on business as partners. The firm was dissolved and the firm was dissolved. The appellant claimed relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, claiming that it had transferred its business to a limited company with effect from November 13, 1947 by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948. The High Court held that the transfer of business was not a change in the constitution of the firm but was merely a change in its constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The appellant was entitled to claim relief under section 24(4) Of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1918. [780 E] (2) The partnership deed did not create any new right or liability. It only provided for the dissolution of the firm. The firm continued to be a limited company. The firm could not be said to have been dissolved before the dissolution. [790 F G] (3) The firm was not a mere change in the Constitution of the firm, but was a change in constitution of the partnership. The firm itself was not a distinct legal entity. The firm had no independent existence. The firm cannot be said to be a separate legal entity. [795 C D] (4) The firm had not been dissolved before its dissolution. The firm ceased to exist after the dissolution. The partnership deed does not create any fresh rights or obligation. [796 A B] (5) The firm is not a mere transfer of the business of the firm to a limited Company. The firm has not been dissolved. The firm continues to be a body corporate. [797 E]
5364: The respondent, an employee of the Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960, was appointed as a part time Assistant Administrative Officer on 1st September, 1956. 3542: The appellants were members of the Bar. The contents of the letter do not bear out anything else. [773B] 4. The letter also refers to the fact that there are certain allegations against the Chief Justice that he is trying to influence the judiciary. [774E F] 5. The letter is an order made by the Chief justice in exercise of its power under section 3 of the Contempt Of Courts Act, and therefore, the same must be construed as having been issued by the Chief Justice. [775F G]
266: The petitioner company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It had two units in its name and one unit in the name of a firm called M/s. R. B. Poddar & Co., and the other unit in the firm name of M/s R. B.. Poddar and Company. In the assessment year 1954 55 the Central Government referred to the Commission for investigation under section 5(1) of the Act and on the 12th April, 1954, the Central Government made an order under section 5 (4) of the , directing that the case be investigated by the Commission. On the 12th of April, 1954 the Central Government issued a notification under section 5A(3) of the . The petitioner company filed a petition before this Court under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification on the ground that the provisions of sections 5(1), 5(4), 6, 7 and 8 of the Act were discriminatory and violative of articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as it contravened articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The Central Government could not issue a notification under article 31(2) of the Indian Constitution without complying with the requirements of article 31(5). The Act is a law relating to income tax and the Central Government has no power to issue a notification in respect of a matter which is covered by article 31(6). The Act does not make any provision for the making of a declaration by the Central Government that any particular property is exempt from income tax. The Act does nothing more than merely enacts that the Central Government may issue a notification declaring that any particular person or class of persons is to be included within the scope of the Act. The Act is not concerned with the classification of persons or things into different classes or categories. The classification must have a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute. The classification can only be based on some rational principle and it must not be arbitrary but must be based upon some real and substantial distinction between the persons grouped together and those who are left out. 2207: The respondent purchased a business of a dealer as defined in the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. He was assessed to sales tax on his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales tax authorities recovered the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the business. The respondent appealed to the Commercial Tax Officer as well as to the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. The respondent took the matter in appeal under the Letters Patent. The High Court held that the State Government had authority under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in respect of the turnover of the transferor. Held, that the respondent was not liable to pay sales tax on the sale of the goods effected by him with effect from the date of transfer of the business under rule 21 A of the Rules framed in exercise of the powers conferred on the State Government by section 19(2) of Act. The transfer of the undertaking of the respondent to the State was not an incident of the contract between the respondent and the State. The transfer was not merely a change of ownership or the transfer of the property in the goods involved in the transaction. The transfer did not amount to any change in the ownership of the goods nor did it amount to a transfer of property in the property in goods within the meaning of section 2(g). The respondent was not entitled to recover the arrears of sales tax from the appellant. The respondent was liable to pay tax only on the sales effected by him after the transfer of his undertaking. The respondent could not be made liable to pay any sales tax on sales effected by the appellant after the transfer.

1406: The appellant was a workman in the respondent Bank. He was dismissed from service under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders on June 21, 1958. 2627: The respondent was a tenant of the appellant 's theatre. On December 1, 1960, the appellant entered into an agreement with the respondent for the sale of the theatre and the respondent agreed to sell the theatre to the appellant on November 27, 1954. The agreement provided that the appellant would pay Rs. 10,000 as advance to the respondent. The respondent paid Rs. 10 per month as advance to be adjusted against the price of the theatre. The appellant objected to the respondent 's claim for Rs. 10.000 by way of advance but the respondent contended that the appellant had no right to raise the question of res judicata in the suit. The Trial Court held that the agreement dated December 1, 1959 was not a lease but only a licence and that the appellant was entitled to rely upon the agreement and the document dated December 1. 1960. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the appellant 'was entitled to lead evidence in support of his plea that the agreement was not a licence but only a lease; that the High court should have decided the question of the res judicata in view of section 28 of the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947, which provides that "no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially heard and finally decided by such Court ". HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in its view that the appellant could not be permitted to lead evidence to prove the agreement dated March 27, 1954, and the document of December 1, 1958, as it stood at the time when the agreement was executed. [440 D] (ii) The High court was wrong in holding that it was open to the parties to adduce evidence in support or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff witnesses. The question whether the legal relationship between the parties was in the nature of a lease or of other character had to be decided at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent decree of the trial court. The Highs Court was wrong in holding that the view which was taken by the Sessions Judge was not justified as the High Court had no occasion to consider the evidence in favour of the accused. The High, Court should have considered the evidence in its proper perspective and should not have relied merely on the evidence of P.W. 1, P.W., 2 and P.W.. 3. [365F G]

2124: The appellant was a member of the Sahas. He claimed to belong to a Scheduled Caste in West Bengal. 4316: The appellant company was a partnership firm. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. They served a Charter of Demands in July, 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless. The appellant 's demand for upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments was rejected by the State Government. The appellant filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision in the wage scales, dearness allowance and house rent allowance granted by the appellant made little impact in neutralising the cost of living. The Union also filed a statement claiming an upwards revision in the wages and dearness allowance granted by it made little impact on in neutralising their earnings. The Tribunal found that it was unable to rely on them as comparable concerns. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has rightly held that the existing rates of dearness allowance and House Rent Allowance granted by the Appellant were fair and equitable. [178C] 2. The Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that the existing rate of dearness allowance was fair and equitable and that it should not be disturbed. [179E] 3. The Tribunal considered it fair in paragraph 23 of its award. It was pointed out that the dearness allowance and the house rent allowance given by the appellant were fair and proper. [177D] 4. The Tribunal did not find any reason to interfere with the award of the Tribunal. [175F] 5. The Tribunal is justified in giving a flat increase of Rs. 150/ in the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. [176G]
314: The appellant was put up for trial before the Court of Sessions for offences under sections 465 and 409 of the Indian Penal Code. He pleaded that he had been falsely implicated in a case instituted by the Government against him, but the prosecution did not adduce any evidence to prove his plea. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary when the act complained of was committed while the accused was engaged in the performance of official duties. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the prosecution having failed to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt, the order of acquittal could not be sustained; (ii) the prosecution was barred by section 197(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code because the sanction was necessary when an offence was committed while he was engaged in performance of official duty; (iii) the prosecution being a public servant was bound to comply with the provisions of section 197(4); (iv) the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond all reasonable doubt; (v) the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt; and (vi) the order of conviction was illegal. HELD : (Per Sarkar and Das Gupta JJ.) (i) The prosecution having failed in proving its case beyond doubt, the conviction of the appellant must be set aside. [1305 D] (ii) The prosecution has failed in proving the existence of a valid sanction under section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The prosecution has also failed to prove that the appellant was guilty of misappropriation of funds. [1306 C D] (iii) The prosecution had failed in proving that the appellant had misappropriated funds belonging to the Government. [1307 E F] (iv) The prosecution was entitled to rely upon the evidence of the appellant as well as the evidence of two witnesses examined by it. The appellant had no opportunity to cross examine them. The prosecution had therefore failed to discharge its burden. [1308 A B] (v) The prosecution cannot succeed in establishing its case beyond a reasonable doubt. [1309 G]
2122: The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and was incorporated in 1961. On June 4, 1965 the Central Government issued an order appointing persons as Inspectors for investigating the affairs of the company. The order was made by the Chairman of the Board on May 19, 1965. The order stated that the Board had decided to appoint a person as Inspector for investigation into the affairs of a company and to report thereon in such manner as the Central Government may direct. The appellant company filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order on the ground that the order was mala fide; that the order having been made at the instance of the shareholders was invalid because it was made by a competent person as the Central Govern ment did not have any power to make the order; that the orders were made by the chairman of the Board without giving the appellant an opportunity of being heard; that the appellant company was not given an opportunity of showing cause against the proposed action; that the Board acted arbitrarily in making the order; and that the order being mala fide was liable to be quashed. 6881: The appellant, a co sharer in the State of Punjab, sold his share to the respondent, a tenant in respect of agricultural land and village immovable property. 415: The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 1951. He challenged his detention by a writ petition in the High Court on the ground that the order of detention was mala fide and that it was passed without any real application of mind by the detaining authority. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of detention is not vitiated merely because the grounds furnished in the affidavit filed in support of the petition were not supplied to him. [385 D] (ii) The right of the detenue to make an effective representation against the order of his detention cannot be taken away by implication. If the detenu makes an express request to the detaining authority for supply of all the material he has to comply with the requirements of law. [386 E] (iii) The right to make a representation is a constitutional right which can be enforced only by the making of an effective representation. If the detaining authority does not furnish the grounds of detention within the time specified in sub section (1) of section 3 of the Act, the order of the detention would be bad. [387 F] (iv) The right conferred on the detenue under Article 22(5) of the Constitution is a valuable right and such a right must be exercised fairly and reasonably. It is not enough to show that the detaining authority did not apply its mind at the time when the order of bail was made. [388 A B] (v) The right guaranteed by Article 22(4) is a valuable one and its exercise cannot be lightly interfered with except on the ground of non communication of the decision of the detaining authority or the grounds of the detention. [389 C] (vi) The right under Article 22 (5) is a constitutional guarantee which means that the person detained should have a reasonable opportunity to know the case against him. The obligation of the detaining Authority to afford the detenu the earliest opportunity to make a 'representation is a Constitutional right. [390 G]
2248: The appellant was a Panchayat and the respondent was its President. [847 E] (2) The Standing Committees had no jurisdiction or authority to decide the appeals on merits as they had failed to specify the octroi limits. 5142: The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was a dangerous person within the meaning of section 2(c) of the . The order of detention was confirmed by the District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner under section 3 (2) of . The detenu filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of detention. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the order of preventive detention could not be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order passed by the District magistrate was bad as the detaining authority had failed to consider the question whether the detenu should be released or not; that the detenu was not served with all the documents referred to and relied on before the detaining authority; that the order was mala fide and was based on conjectures and surmises; that the detaining authority did not apply its mind to the facts mentioned in the grounds of detention; that the representation made by the detenu was rejected by the State Government without any application of mind; that the detention order was illegal because the detenu was denied an opportunity to make a representation which was not considered at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive custody cannot be sustained against a person who is already in prison. [911B] 2.1 The order of the District Magistrate does not disclose that the detenu had been informed that he was likely to be released from detention. It merely states that the detenu may make a representation to the Advisory Board. [912C D] 2.2 The order of bail passed by the High Court was not proper. [913D] 3.1 The detenu was in jail when the order of his detention was passed. He was not in jail. The order was passed after considering the report of the Advisory Board and the materials placed before it. The order also does not indicate that the detenu has been furnished with copies of the reports. [914E F] 4.1 The detaining authority must consider the fact that the detenu is already in jail.
2065: The appellants were the trustees of a temple in which the respondents were appointed as trustees. The temple was managed by a committee consisting of the manager and two other members of the committee, who had been appointed as trustees by the committee. The committee was constituted for the management of the temple and its properties. The committee had granted to the respondents certain properties in favour of the temple. The respondents claimed that they had acquired title to the properties in suit and a permanent injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with their possession of the same. The trial court held that the respondents had proved their title to the property in suit and that the appellants had failed to prove that they had transferred the properties in favour the respondents. On appeal, the District Judge held that the appellants could not be said to have acquired title to any part of the properties in dispute. In second appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had failed to establish that the transfer effected by the manager of the temple in favour of respondents was invalid. It also held that the evidence adduced by the respondents did not prove the existence of any temple in favour or that the transfer was made on the basis of the alleged transfer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether a transfer effected by a manager of a temple is valid must depend upon the facts of each case. [801 B] (2) The question as to whether a transfer can be regarded as an alienation of the property belonging to the temple has to be decided on the basis that the transfer is made by the manager himself. If it is shown that the transfer has been made by the Manager himself, then the question of proving that the transfer does not amount to a transfer of the property belongs to the manager. [802 C D] (3) The question about the validity of a transfer may be determined only after the enquiry into the genuineness of the transaction is completed. But if the transfer is found to be invalid, the question of title cannot arise until the enquiry is over. [803 A] (4) The question of title to the lands in suit is a mixed question of fact and law and the finding of the courts below on such questions would not be open to challenge under article 136 of the Constitution. [804 E F]

The appellants contended that the Custodian had no power under section 12 of the , to cancel the lease granted by them, and that the respondent was not entitled to evict the appellants from the mills. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal held that section 12 applied only to properties belonging to the evacuee and that the movables in respect of which directions were given by the Custodian were unauthorised. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Custodian had power under section 10 to cancel the leases granted by him; (ii) the direction with reference to the appellants was beyond the jurisdiction conferred upon him by section 10 of the Act, and (iii) the order of the Custodian was without jurisdiction. HELD : (i) The power under section 11 is a judicial power and the Custodian has power to issue the directions under section 12. [851 G] (ii)The power under section 13 is a judicial one and the Custodian can exercise the same powers as the Custodian under section 12(1). [852 C D] (iii)Section 12 applies only to properties of the evacuee and not to property of the evacuee. It does not apply to any property belonging to the appellants. [853 E] (iv)The power of the Custodian under sections 12 and 13 is a quasi judicial power and he cannot pass an order which would be outside the scope of section 12. He can only act under section 12 and not under section 13. [854 F] (v)The power to cancel the agreement to sell is a judicial function and the Custodian could not pass an order under section 12 without his consent. [855 A B] (vi)The power conferred by section 12 is a judicial or quasi-judicial power and the exercise thereof must be subject to the restrictions imposed by section 10. [856 C] (vii)The power is a judicial act and the Custodian cannot pass an interim order under section 10. The Custodian can pass such orders as he thinks fit. [857 D]
7109: The appellant was the owner of a land in Rajasthan. The Sub Divisional Officer held that Surendrapal Singh, (appellant) aged about 25 years, was a minor son of Raghubir Singh and used to 725 study in Punjab and further held that the land in possession of Raghubirs Singh was ancestral. The Sub Division Officer, Hanumanganj, by his order dated 5th May 1976 held that Surenderpal Singh was a minor and used to look after his mother and children. The Sub Divisonal Officer, Hanuangarh, by his orders dated 10th August, 1972, determined the ceiling area and directed that the ceiling area be determined according to the old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to the new law i. e. Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973. The Sub divisional Officer, by his revisional order dated 6th August, 1977 set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer and restored the order of Sub Divisional Officer. The Board of Revenue, however, set aside the appellate order of the Collector and restored the original order of the Tehsildar. The Board, therefore, passed an order on 30th September, 1979, setting aside the order dated 5 th May, 1976 of the Sub Divisonary Officer and remanding the case to him for deciding the question as to whether the land in question was ancestral or not. The Board also held that the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside the orders of the Sub Divisional Officer and the revenue appellate authority under Section 221 of the Act. The Board accordingly set aside the said order and remanded the matter to the Sub Divisioinal Officer for determination of the ceiling area afresh. The Board took the view that the Board of revenue had no jurisdiction over the matter and the Board of Revenues could not set up the powers of superintendence and control over the Board of the Revenue

1762: The respondent was a resident of the former State of Dholpur and the dispute which led to the suit out of which appeal No. 887 was filed by the respondent against the State of Rajasthan. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No, 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. The respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni with a further sum of Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. He also deposited Rs. 30 as export duty in Advance Licence. In June 1947 the respondent applied for a permit for import of 15,500 maunds from the former Part B State of Rajasthan and the appellant refused it. On August 15, 1947 the appellant wrote to the respondent stating that he had no objection if the respondent was allowed to export 15,000 munds of Chuni with a similar stipulation that the respondent would not claim any refund of the amount paid by him till the end of September 1947. The respondent contended that in view of article 295(2) of the Constitution the State of Rajpramukh was bound by the obligations of the former Part C State of Rajasthan until the merger of the former part of India in the new Part B State. Held: (i) Article 295(1) of the constitution is not applicable to the present case because the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of the covenant entered into between the parties. The covenant was not void or inoperative but was merely an agreement to merge the former Part A State of Rajasthan with the new Part C State. (ii)The respondent was not liable to pay the amount of Rs. 15,000/in lieu of the contract price. The respondent was not bound by the covenant.

The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the Act and Rules had come into force in Ramanathapuram District on January 1, 1953, and directing the respondents to forbear from enforcing any or all the provisions of that Act as amended and the Rules and bylaws framed thereunder. 4782: The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Sub Judge, against the appellant Corporation and the Divisional Manager of Masulipatam Branch of the Corporation for recovery of Rs. 50,000 as damages on account of medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased. 2657: The appellant was the plaintiff in a suit for recovery of money. The respondent obtained an order of stay under section 19(1) of the . The appellant applied to the High Court for a certificate under Arts.133(1)(a) and 133(1)(b) of the Constitution, which was granted. The High Court held that an order granting interim injunction "is a final order, as far as this Court is concerned, determining the rights of parties within this Court 's jurisdiction, determined the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; if the rights of both parties are identical, the Court has no power to grant the certificate. Held, that the order granting interim injunctions is not a final order within the meaning of article 133(1) (a). The expression "final order" means a final order. In the present case not only the order of the High Court amounts to a judgment or a decree, but also a final order on the merits of the case. The order does not amount to a final order because it merely decides some questions of law arising between the parties. It does not finally determine what the rights of one party stand or what is called the subject matter of the dispute in the suit or proceeding. The order merely determines what the rights in dispute in the court of first instance and still remain to be tried. The order cannot be said to be final when it decides certain rights of the other party.
4807: The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974. He was promoted as a clerk on April 1, 1975 and continued to work as such till March 14, 1976. The fact that the appellant was promoted as head clerk on April 2, 1976 would not make any difference because the appellant was given the benefit of the service rendered by him in the Panchayat Samiti from April 1, 1974 to March 14, 1977. 4451: The appellant, a Hindu, was the owner of certain properties in village Shiv Dass in the district of Banaras. He purchased them from the personal and separate funds of his father and also from the personal funds of his brother. The income from these properties was received by him as a trustee for the Math. The income was applied to the maintenance of the Math and its properties. The income of the Math was not utilised for the purpose of the Math but was utilised for the purposes of the Math itself. The High Court held that the income was not the personal property of the Math or the deity and that the income must be regarded as the personal property. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The income from the properties belonging to the Math was held by the Math as the personal income of the Mahant. The income so derived was applied to religious and charitable objects. [875 C] (ii) The income was not a personal income of a person. It was a personal income. The income did not cease to be the personal income merely because the Math was a public trust. [876 D] (iii) The income of a Math is not a personal property of a person within the meaning of section 2(13)(iv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The income is not a part of the personal income. [877 E] (iv) The income is a personal income and the income cannot be said to be the income of the institution. [878 F] (v) The income has been applied to religious, charitable and other objects of the Math. [879 B]
1181: The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village Raikot. They made an application for consolidation of their lands with those of the appellants in the village. The Assistant Custodian rejected the applications on the ground that no land was available in the village in view of the fact that the land had been allotted to the appellants in lieu of their land at the time of allotment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the cancellation in question was not a mere mistake or error committed by the Custodian while granting the quasi permanent allotment in favour the appellants. HELD: (i) The cancellation in question is not a mere change of opinion but a decision arrived at after full consideration of the relevant material. [336 D] (ii) The cancellation was not a bona fide one. It was a decision based on the facts found by the authorities concerned. [347 A B] (iii) The cancellation of the quasi permanent allotments in favour of appellants was not merely a change of opinion. The cancellation was a decision founded upon the facts found in the records of the case. [348 C] (iv) The cancellation is not a result either of misapplication of the principles of natural justice or fraud. [349 E]
3292: The appellant was the Mahant of a Dera. He died on 13 10 1970 leaving behind him his legal representatives. The appellant had raised an alternative contention before the High Court that there was no cause of action for the suit. It is obvious from the facts that the appellant did not raise any such contention at the time when the suit was instituted. [821F G] 4. The appellant was not a party to a suit. His right to sue would arise only if he succeeds in proving his title to the property. [822G] 5. The appellant cannot be said to have acquired any interest in any property by reason of his being a person who claimed to be the head of the Dera. The appellant has no right to sue. [883B] 7. The appellant must succeed in his own right. [884D] 8. The appellant may be entitled to file an appropriate proceeding for setting aside the abatement of the suit but the appellant cannot be permitted to take advantage of his own wrong
4917: The petitioners were working as Lecturers in the Government Higher Secondary School and Junior Colleges. The Government has power under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Education Act, 1982 to fix the age of a person at 55 years. It is not necessary that the Government should have consulted the Board or the Government itself before fixing the age. [560C] 2. The Government cannot take any action without consulting the Board or Government themselves. The Government can only act after consultation with the Board or government itself. [561D] 3. The Government is entitled to take such measures as are deemed necessary by them. [562E] 4. The Government may exercise its powers arbitrarily but not arbitrarily so as to bring about a total disinclination to the public services. [563F] 5. The Government must act fairly and reasonably. 6622: The appellant was a dealer in milk and milk products. He purchased certain goods from the respondent for sale to a dealer who had sold them to another dealer. 1329: The respondent was a dealer in cotton and castor oil. He claimed exemption from sales tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947 on the ground that he had not passed on the shipment of goods to the buyers at any point of time before the shipment. The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed him to purchase tax on a taxable turnover including these sales. The respondent moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of assessment and the notice of demand. The High Court held that the sale was "in the course of export" and the sales were "in the nature of "sale" within the meaning of article 286(1)(b). In appeal by special leave, Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of article 286 (1)(b) of Constitution. The words "in the present sales the property in the goods passed " in article 286(2) are used in a wider sense and include the sale in the course of import as well as in the course.of export. The word "in the same way" means "in the process of being exported". The word "import" is used in the wider sense and includes the movement of goods from one State to another or from one State into another. The word 'import' in its widest sense means "to bring into existence new goods from one state to another." The word "intra-State" in article 286 (3) of the Constitution means "to bringing into existence new and distinct goods from one another, whether or not there is a direct and proximate connection between the two" and does not mean "import", and the word "imported" in the context must be construed accordingly.

The Explanation further states that where a divorced woman is unable to pay maintenance to her legally wedded wife, such woman can also be granted maintenance from her husband if he has sufficient means of livelihood. [803B C] 4. The Explanation

4480: The appellant, a Government Company incorporated under the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, was constituted under section 65 of the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation Act. 1956. The appellant, the Government Company was incorporated under the Madhya Pradesh Act, 1956. The Government of Madhya Pradesh issued a notification dated February 27, 1976, under section 67(1) of the Madhya Pashu Pravesh Pariyojana Adhiniyam, 1961, exempting certain properties from the levy of property tax on the ground that the said properties were situated within the limits of the Municipality. The appellant challenged the validity of the aforesaid notification by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the exemption granted to the properties of the appellant was not valid and quashed the notification. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The exemption granted to properties of the Government Company is not valid because the exemption granted is only for the purpose of levying the tax. [9D] (2) The exemption given to the properties is not for the purpose specified in section 68 but for the purpose mentioned in section 69. The exemption is for the purpose for which it is granted. Therefore, the exemption granted cannot be sustained. [10E] (3) The exemption is granted for the purpose other than the purpose for the construction of houses or buildings for the use of the public. [11F] (4) The exemption does not extend to the purpose for constructing houses or buildings. It extends to the purpose of constructing houses or houses. [12B] (5) The exemption cannot be extended to the purpose mentioned under section 68. [13C] (6) The exemption can be extended to a particular purpose.
